utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case, IT-05-88/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, madam registrar. First the Chamber apologises for the late start, but that's due to the fact that a confidential filing of last Friday reached us only 20 minutes ago, and there the Chamber considered it wiser to first get an impression of what was written in the French language. Before we continue, could we have the appearances? Prosecution, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. Susan Somers for the Prosecution. To my immediate right, Janet Stewart, case manager; to my left, Mr. Aleksandar Kontic; behind me to my right, Mr. Kweku Vanderpuye; and to my left behind me, Mr. Peter McCloskey, senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Piletta-Zanin on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbic, I would just like to verify whether you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I turn, because we are in a video link with Sarajevo, I turn to those present in Sarajevo to introduce themselves. Could I have the appearances on behalf of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning from Sarajevo. The delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is grateful to the Referral Chamber of the ICTY for enabling us to participate in this hearing via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for the assistance of the technicians for the following reason. The volume of the words spoken in Sarajevo are such that I failed to understand the translation. Yes, I see. I could have done it myself. May I invite you to reintroduce yourself in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning from Sarajevo. On behalf of the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina we would like to thank the Referral Chamber of the ICTY for enabling us to participate in this hearing via videolink. The delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprises to my right, Ms. Natasa Vukovic, registry office for section I and II of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. To my left is Mr. Emir Neradin, registry office for section I and II for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Kwai Hong Ip representing the Prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My name is Milana Popadic, Ministry of Justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Although Mr. Ibro Bulic was announced, he was unable it attend, and he also works for the Prosecution's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Popovic. I suggest to the parties that we proceed in the following way: I first give an opportunity to both Prosecution and Defence and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to make any submissions in addition to what has already been submitted in writing. I also draw the attention of the parties and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the fact that some of the written submissions were filed confidentially, which might cause a need to go into private session or closed session. Whenever there is any need to do so, please inform me and we will proceed upon the basis of a decision of such a request. Ms. Somers, may -- before I invite you to make any further submissions, have you received the latest Defence filing, the confidential filing of last Friday that was filed at three minutes past 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we received it, we haven't received any form of translation so as to be able to discuss it amongst ourselves. But those of us who read some French have gone through it, but I cannot say it has been studied as we would have like to have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Popadic, may I ask you, whether you received this last filing in the French language, which is of course one of the official languages of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just seen the filing for the first time now. I had no occasion to see it earlier, and I don't think that any members of our delegation saw it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the best way of proceeding is that I give an opportunity to the parties and the government to give any further submissions, and that we would then have a break and in this break that the parties and the representatives of the government would have the opportunity to consider the submissions made and include then also to more thoroughly study the submissions made by the Defence. I've read them in French, and I think as a matter of fact that we could proceed at this moment on the basis of just some general information without knowing all the details. Ms. Somers, do you have any idea on how much time you would need to address the Chamber with any additional submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: First, thank you very much for allowing us to have additional submissions. We would request, as we have done in the past and has been permitted, to reserve until all the other parties or invitees have given their submissions. We stand, of course, on what we have submitted but I'm sure there will be comment afterward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the Defence to make any additional submissions, the Chamber would like to turn into closed session. Yes, private session might do as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I complete what I intended to say and clarify something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact I interrupted you because I thought there might be some misunderstanding. If there is anything you would like to deal with confidentially, if it is about health or if it is about the other issue I raised, which certainly is something that would require a closed session or a private session, but let me first confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbic, we'll give you an opportunity to continue, and whenever there would be any need to go into private session, please address me and then we will decide. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. When speaking of the written submissions I was referring to the material of the 1st of June. I didn't even know about this motion of Friday or the one of the 14th of June. I wish to point out, Your Honours, that I never saw this submission, and that it was done without my knowledge. I don't know why confidential motions are filed without my knowing about them. Also, I wish to say that my only communication with my counsel was by way of telegram with completely unclear contents, and visits of half an hour or 40 minutes. I have all these telegrams here, and from them my attitude to 11 bis is quite clear. You may see them, Your Honours. I was very surprised by the threats made to me about the threats to my personal security. These are letters I received on the 6th of November and 21st of November, and it was also confirmed to me orally during the visit of the 23rd of November. He is probably doing this based on information he has or in order to intimidate me, but I refuse to accept any kind of intimidation or blackmail. All this shows what kind of legal assistance I am getting from my counsel. I have all the evidence before me, and it is available for your inspection. Your Honours, the crucial point I wish to draw attention to are the threats concerning my fitness to stand trial and my mental health. I wish to say that I am in good health, and that I am able to follow any proceedings before any court against me. So there is no justification in linking this with my case. Doctors are superficial, in my case. Please refer my case under 11 bis. Let me be tried there, if I am guilty. Thank you for your understanding and your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that although the submissions of the 18th of May and the 1st of June were not ex parte but were confidential, that they were not communicated to the representatives of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Chamber instructs the Registry at this moment to communicate these filings as well to the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, still being confidential filings, but that the representatives should be aware of the content of it. Therefore, at this moment, we have three series of documents. The first the May/June submissions by the Registry to be communicated to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Second category is the request and the response by the Registry for further submissions of November 2006 to be communicated to the parties and to the representatives of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally, the submission filed on Friday, the 12th of January by counsel to -- well, it is available already to the parties, but they should try to get acquainted with the context -- content of this submission written in French as soon as possible. Could I just ask Ms. Somers, how much time would you consider you would need to make yourself acquainted with this material?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have reviewed the French language filing of my learned counsel opposite, but I have not had a chance to study the submissions. Yes, I would be grateful for that. And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, until 11. Of course I gave a short summary of it, but of course I fully understand that you would like to read it and not rely on any summary provided by the Chamber. Until 11.00, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I would be grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'm very sorry, but I am supposed to be in Geneva, I am being expected there and French is one of official languages in this Tribunal. In other words, Mr. Trbic said "yes" three times, maybe rightly or wrongly, but I am driving back to Geneva, I would like not to have to drive all night because simply somebody can't read one of the official languages of the Tribunal. It's very strange. You were kind enough to convey to me a decision dated 24th November 2006. I was given this in English. Can I ask for a French version of it? That would be very helpful. Failing this, well, that would be just another case of having no translation; that wouldn't be a problem. But 11.00, that's a long time to read a few pages. I am quite willing to translate them to the Prosecution if they want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless you're asking for a French version at the same time you are offering a French-English translation to the Prosecution. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is not the first time we meet each other. I am aware that you are mastering of the English language is such that even without a French version of this document you would be well in a position to be acquainted with the content and just as you expect from the Prosecution to be able to read a French document, one of the official languages, isn't it true that when you are able to read and to speak English, that you could work on the basis of an English document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President, and you are aware of it. This is a question of principle. It is not up to me, maybe there is in my staff people who are only French speaking and that's not the problem, and you know that very well. You too are quite master of the French language, and that's fine. But simply everybody has to take into account everybody else's interest. I came by car this time and, for once, I would like the Prosecution to be kind enough not to waste time uselessly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I take it you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will shorten the time a bit, but not until after I've asked Sarajevo, because they still have to be -- the documents still have to be communicated to Sarajevo, which might take a bit more time than communication here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just let the Chamber -- referral bench be aware, it is not the French language issue that requires for us the chance to study it, it is simply the Registry documents. We are well able to go through the French submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you give us any impression on how much time it would take to communicate the relevant documents to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will adjourn until -- on the basis of the understanding that most of the documents have been already communicated to Sarajevo, we will adjourn until 10 minutes to 11.00 and then we'll hear from the parties whether they are sufficiently prepared. We stand adjourned. --- Break taken at 10.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber would like to go into private session for perhaps another couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would like to give you an opportunity first, since the Prosecution has asked the Chamber to consider it a practical way of proceeding whether you would like to make any additional submissions in addition to what you have submitted already in writing to the Chamber in respect of the 11 bis request.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you know how fond I am of principles. Before I can answer, maybe we should have asked the representatives of the government whether they've been able to have access in a language they understand to my filings of yesterday. Because if they have had access to these filings, we would gain a lot of time. If it's not the case, then I would make a brief summary that would be translated for everyone including those who do not master the French language perfectly. And then we would move quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the break the Chamber has considered the importance of the representatives of the government to be fully informed because much of your submission is a reference to what the government submitted itself. So therefore it doesn't give much new information. And the point which is not of extreme relevance for the government is that Mr. Trbic himself would like to be referred as soon as possible, and I mentioned that before. So you may proceed at this moment, but I will certainly ask at a later stage the government whether they had an opportunity to read your submission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to be rather brief. The problem we are faced with is not the person of Mr. Trbic when you consider his quality as a subject of law, as a subject of law who might be transferred. Because everybody here agrees that Mr. Trbic was not a member and is not a member of the group called the most senior leaders. And if you consider his rank, because he was not even an officer, he was under the orders of a lieutenant. And if you also look at the facts, that his acts, his participation, his effective participation, according to the text usually applied here, obviously Mr. Trbic is a subject of law who can be transferred, and he has repeatedly asked to be transferred. As counsel I have taken note of the position of the government, including in the Popovic case, because right from the beginning Mr. Trbic requested this case not to be severed, he wanted to take part right from the beginning. Personally I asked for the case to be suspended. But I take note of the fact that the ad hoc commission, that the government and the government itself believe that this case, because of the very nature of the crime involved, this case is not -- cannot be referred, transferred. We have a situation where the crime itself, the genocide and the joint criminal enterprise, have not been resolved by any authority, by any referral bench in this Tribunal. Undeniably genocide is such a grave crime that the question now has been posed, and obviously the answer cannot be an easy one. However, it is also obvious when you read the latest report of Mr. -- of the president of the Tribunal, Mr. Pocar, it is obvious that the Tribunal will close by the year 2010, and the best things in life have to have an end at some point, everybody will go home then. But we are not certain, we cannot be certain when we look at the calender, that the Tribunal will have the means, will have -- will lead the necessary policy to try this man, although he should have been tried with other people, but that's the remit of the Prosecution. So the question that is being asked is a practical question. It's not a legal question. What are we going to do with this man when you consider one of the most fundamental principles, which is not only that of a fair trial but that of the expeditious trial. Because according to my information -- I repeat, according to my information, apparently he could not be tried here before two -- two years, two years, that's 2008 if there is no delay, maybe 2009. Is that a not normal situation? It is up to you to give an answer to that question. Furthermore, if -- if, and I insist on the word "if" because Mr. Trbic has always said he is in perfectly good mental health. But if -- if we were in a situation where an accused was not fully fit mentally speaking, then as far as I understand in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Sarajevo, there is no organisation, there is no institution that is able to deal with such a matter. I was also given to understand that there is no will to have someone who is prosecuted for genocide being made to work for -- being made to do community work. In both cases we -- because this case was disjoined -- or severed from the Popovic case, we are placed today in an impossible situation. If you grant the referral that is being requested by Mr. Trbic and, as his lawyer, I cannot do anything else, then you will go against the jurisprudence because of the gravity of the crime involved. If you decide against the referral, then there will be very few solutions available. As a result, and as I have said before as Defence counsel, I cannot -- I can only -- as a lawyer I can only refer you to the application of the principles that govern the referral of a case when you are dealing with two matters, the first being the genocide and the second being the fact that this genocide is alleged to have been committed as part of a general criminal enterprise. Obviously I cannot rule on that myself, as otherwise technically speaking Mr. Trbic is an acceptable candidate for a referral. If you look at his place in the structure involved and if you look at his participation in the crime, but let me add that he has always denied and rejected the charges brought against him. Therefore, the position is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me to interrupt you. First of all, most what you said is not in addition to your written submission, but repeats your written submissions. I now see that since you are revisiting the genocide and joint criminal enterprise and participation in the joint criminal enterprise, that it is not only in your written submission, you dealt with it at an earlier stage of your submission today, and now you are revisiting that matter. So there are three times. Could you please wind up and come to a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I was -- I was -- I just concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Then I would like to turn to you, Ms. Popadic. First of all, did you have an opportunity to -- to read, and if not personally, to have explained what is found in the submissions I referred to earlier, that is May, June, November, and last Friday, the 12th of January submission by Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. During the break we received all three of these submissions. The ones from May and June we studied in detail and the one that was filed on Friday we only had the contents of it briefly explained to us so that the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after becoming acquainted with these filings, remains by its written reply submitted in our earlier filing. If necessary today we can provide additional clarifications or additional responses to some other questions. And if we are unable to answer any of the questions today, given the filings we received during the break, we reserve the right to provide written answers at a later stage. Once again, I would like to emphasise that in view of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this particular case would not be suitable for referral to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina for two reasons. The first being the criteria of the gravity of the crime which is not in compliance with the provisions of Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and its implementation so far. The second reason is this: If the accused became mentally ill following the commission of a crime or if the crime was committed when the accused was of unsound mind or was temporarily insane, that would be another reason. When it comes to the first reason the position of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina is such that the crimes that this particular accused is being charged with fall into the category of the most grave crimes. We heard that the Defence shares this view, and in our opinion this does not comply with the criteria envisaged in Rule 11 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting our colleagues in BiH, but we request that this be in open session, as opposed to closed session, if we're still in closed. I'm not clear. Are we in open?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, we are -- we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you can confirm that, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Popadic, the Prosecution wanted to verify whether we are in open session. May I invite you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this case has been severed from the Popovic et al case, we believe that it needs to be assessed in comparison with the case from which it was severed. The Popovic case in the pre-trial stage -- or, rather, the Popovic case is in the trial stage now, and this accused stands accused for the same facts as those in the indictment in the Popovic case. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina believes that the crimes that this accused stands indicted for in the confirmed indictment taken within their legal qualification from the indictment do not fall in the category of crimes under Rule 11 bis and, as such, they make this case inappropriate for referral under Rule 11 bis. Furthermore, when it comes to the responsibility of the accused, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina believes that this particular case could be referred to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina because this particular accused does not fall in the category of the perpetrators at the highest levels who are most responsible for crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the ICTY. We saw that the Defence shares this view. As for the second reason, which goes against the possibility of referring this case, is the mental health of the accused. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina believes that if the accused suffers from a mental illness or rather started suffering from a mental illness after the crime was committed or started suffering in the course of the trial, the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in both of these instances would refer this case to the competent social work or social services centre, in which case the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina would no longer have the jurisdiction over this case, and the competent social services within the relevant entity would gain the jurisdiction over this case. The social services centre, as it stands now, are faced with a situation where there is -- where there are significant difficulties with medical facilities and their resources. We do have adequate mental facilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we do have some, but they do not have all the necessary resources in order to deal with these cases. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina thus believes that this particular case is not suitable for referral to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Rule 11 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Popadic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this case is not complicated. Any complications that have been brought or allegedly brought before this Referral Bench are creations based on speculation and I must say contradictory positions to former submissions both by BiH and failure to look at the correct state of the jurisprudence. First, working backward, the issue of mental health is at best speculative. It has been raised in a way that has not forced any formal hearing. The issues which have been considered essential for assessment of capacities, based on the Strugar decision, to the extent the accused was willing to undertake them in examination are addressed, and I would draw Your Honour's attention to those. I think they're very telling. The observations which were relied on also in the Strugar decision by the demeanour of the accused in proceedings, I think, are also very telling. So although none of us professes to have the ability to be a mental health worker, we are suggesting that there is really no issue but speculative matters that have spun out of control and have now become used as a basis for effectively shirking responsibility that any national system would have to undertake if it were to conduct trials seriously in the criminal law. What we are hearing is that should a -- an accused before a state court judge, find himself in a state of unfitness, even after commencement of trial, that that would paralyse the system. This is highly unlikely in light of the international standards that have been accorded or the recognition of having international standards that have been accorded to the state court. We remind -- which I'm sure we don't need to remind, the Bench is well aware that the Detention Unit has been certified as meeting international standards in BiH. So all of this suggests that either there is some problem that was not dealt with, or that it may be inconvenient, but we take our accused as we find them in all systems, whether the incapacity, which is not in any way, not only not confirmed, but has not gone beyond the level of mere speculation, were to eventualise, or before a trial, before a referral, or during the course of trial. Secondly, and perhaps importantly, I will avoid at this moment the issue of -- issues that have to go into private session, but the documents that we read over the course of the break in no way change the position. In fact, speculative. The Chamber heard from the accused on the issues, and there was nothing of any concrete nature. If the Referral Bench wishes to hear from any other member of the Prosecution as to these issues, they are present and can certainly offer input rather than have counsel speak for his feeling about what the Prosecution may or may not hold as its position. Importantly, the level of the accused all agree is proper. Defence, the accused, and the Prosecution agree that the case should go to BH. BH's assertion now, as to the arguments of gravity are simply disingenuous. BH is trying cases now concerning the Srebrenica material, the counts, the allegations in Srebrenica, and I would find it very difficult to accept that should we have never, in the Tribunal, should this institution never have asserted its primacy, that the Bosnians are now saying that they would not have undertaken to try genocide cases, given that genocide has been a crime on its books, even dating back to the socialist codes and currently is a crime. In fact, they are trying Srebrenica cases now. The jurisprudence in no way bars a referral. If one were to look at even at the language of, let's say, a Dragomir Milosevic denial, that does not say that you have to have both, it talks about a balance. And in fact, Ademi Norac involved a brigadier and a colonel. The balance that is struck by examining the totality, not in isolation, but the totality of what is before the Bench in the indictment governs. The actual Security Council resolutions do not talk -- 1503 and 1534 do not address severity they address all -- indicted before this Tribunal are by definition serious violations of international and humanitarian law and, yes, they include genocide and, yes, Bosnia can avail itself equally well Krstic adjudicated facts and find itself not at all disadvantaged. The actual addressed points are the level of the accused, mid -- I'm sorry, intermediate to lower level. In fact, I remind this Chamber of its very well reasoned decision in Mejakic, which was a joint criminal enterprise indictment which represents one of the most horrific crimes ever to have taken place, a series of crimes ever to have taken place in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or anywhere for that matter, and that case is being tried in the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In fact, it involved enormous numbers of human beings, it involved a period of time, and it also involved what was a joint criminal enterprise, and that has been no bar. In this instance, given, as the Chamber -- as the Bench will look at all factors, the level which we agree is appropriate, and the -- I'm sorry, the -- yes, the level which is appropriate and the gravity which Bosnia itself undertakes to try, there can be no question but that it can and should be sent down. Again, there is absolutely no basis for giving this case any more concern than any other case where there are issues raised. For example, in the extreme, on mental health issues, that is something Bosnia will have to deal with if it expects to be a player in the international community and it has so far demonstrated it can. It is on notice that it must do what it has to do. Again, it is unlikely that in connection with this accused that will arise, from on things we've seen. But should it, in order for it to be considered seriously for referrals, it will have to comport with all international standards. It is simply inconceivable that a sovereign system would rule out not just the possibility but given a sovereign system in a formerly war-torn area, the possibility of any incapacity, particularly one resulting allegedly from any mental issues in its scheme. Excuse me just a minute, Your Honour. We are not in agreement with the submission of the Registrar to the extent that there can be confirmation of the level of general protection, then it may be appropriate for further discussions. But in no institution is there an absolute guarantee -- in no institution is there an absolute guarantee of security, even in this one. In no institution is there a guarantee of a person retaining his or her balance at all times. I do draw the attention of the Chamber, by the way -- to the Referral Bench, excuse me, to various pronouncements by the very well established psychiatrist in the Strugar case, Dr. Matthews, depression being a natural expectation of custody. In terms of issues, should -- now this may -- this may or may not be appropriate for closed or private session. I think in an abundance of caution I would ask that we do go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the Chamber would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In summary, by virtue of the mandate that we have to conclude the work of the Tribunal, and by virtue of what has already been undertaken by the court in BH indicating that it can and essentially, if referred, will try this case. Its level of comfort or not in maybe the amount of work that has to be done is not a determining factor. All of us face that, whether it is here or there. Certainly their work is easier by virtue of having the other cases to rely on. The ability of the system to adapt itself to a speedy trial system is very favourable. Mr. Rosovic also opted to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina because he wanted a speedy trial. It is certainly not an unusual approach to take and it is to be commended when all other things are equal. In our position all other things are equal when there is nothing unusual that has been raised in this case that should bar referral, including the gravity. As time progresses toward our conclusion, it is clear, unless Bosnia is saying it is not prepared to handle genocide cases or any allegations, then that has to be dealt with by its own sovereign structures and their responsibility to their people to tell them that they are not prepared to do that. At this point, we feel that we have made well the case for referral, that should there be any further questions that the Bench might wish to put to my colleagues, we are prepared to answer them. And we thank you and urge that the case be referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A brief question, Ms. Somers. My question is related to the severance of Mr. Trbic which is pending before the Appeals Chamber. Do you think or argue that referral can be ordered irrespective of the outcome of the Appeals Chamber's decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may take a moment to speak with Mr. McCloskey as to the status of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate it, I was trying to get up to speed on what the status is. It is unclear why, quite frankly an issue of severance is taking so long. So it would be prudent to resolve it so that we that this is, in fact, the indictment. But a request, certainly 11 bis matters are fast-track appeals matters and perhaps because it has such a close link to 11 bis, it may be a matter that the bureau may find wishes to ask for resolution. It would seem wise, and certainly helpful for clarity, so that all know exactly what indictment we are proceeding on, to have it done. But again, that is a matter sadly outside of our hands. We -- but we would urge any remedy that may be available through -- through Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I wanted to hear from you is that as a matter of law that whether referral can be ordered without severance at all. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. That is, I think, a legal issue that we're not -- we don't know. The -- me reaction would be that we should wait. That if the work of the appellate chamber is to be viewed as serious, we should wait. Though the practical situation, as we -- as you and I both know, the case that it -- that he would be sent back to has -- has put on so much evidence that it would be hard to imagine a -- in a practical sense, a rejoinder of that case. So I think legally we don't know the answer to your question, but I would think common sense tells us we shouldn't do anything until the appeals is through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The practical problems is that the Appeals Chamber's procedures are suspended pending the competency issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I address that, Your Honour? That -- that should not have been a basis, in my submission, for suspending any provision. Competency can certainly move forward. Appeals can go; competency may or may not, particularly where 11 bis is concerned. It does not have the impact of preventing a referral. So if the bench has not been sufficiently concerned to -- and I don't mean this Bench, if the Trial Chamber has not felt the need to resolve the issue immediately of competency, which is a matter of hearing, of course this Chamber, under 11 bis H is fully empowered to hear the issue of competency, as it can hear any matter before a Trial Chamber, should that really be what is at issue. It should not -- again so many things become interrelated where if they would just be dealt with in order, it would be helpful, but the competency per se should not affect the issue of severance, and competency does not affect the issue of referral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may put a follow-up question there. What if the severance issue had never been raised? I mean, 11 bis request was prior to the severance request, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I believe it was first severed and then 11 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that. I thought it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it always helps to check, but I'm -- I'm -- well, I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that Mr. Piletta-Zanin will assist us in finding answers to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, in relation to this answer, it is in my request that it was severed because I said then there can be no talk of a referral without a prior severance. So that was the chronology, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So my chronology was the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also remind you that for example in situations -- not in this case, but in a general situation where a plea is involved, one can have a plea agreement with -- even though an accused is part of a greater group of accused, and then a severance would certainly be appropriate at the time the cases are severed. In this instance, the timing - and I am grateful to my colleague for clarifying that - should not be a bar, and in fact if the Chamber wants to have anything examined it would certainly request -- I think it would probably be the most appropriate inquiry as to if it believes it should move forward with the Appeals Chamber to so make the request I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not suggesting anything at the moment, but from what I understand, the request dates from the 4th of May of this year [sic], whereas the severance motion of the OTP was of the 16th of June and the severance was I think decided on the 26th of June. What you said, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I leave that open at this moment who specifically asked for the severance, whether it was the Prosecution or the Defence. But at least it seems to be clear that a referral request was there, but there was no mentioning anything -- no mention at all about severance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It might be tidier, but I don't know that it's legally necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least -- then -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do you allow me to say a few words, because I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have in mind to complete the questions of the bench and then to give a new round, five to six minutes, to make any additional submissions the parties would like to make, also in relation to the questions posed by the Bench. I would like to briefly address you, Ms. Popadic, on the following issue: You said that if an accused turns out to be mentally ill, that he would then be within the jurisdiction of the social care authorities. Which suggests that they would not be within the jurisdiction of the state court anymore. I think that's what you said. Isn't it true that if someone recovers from a mental illness that he would then return into the jurisdiction of the state court, so for purposes of trial he would always be in the jurisdiction of the -- under the jurisdiction of the state court?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is any doubt or if there is -- if there are grounds to suspect that an accused cannot participate in a trial because of mental illness, forensic medical opinion will be sought. If it is established by forensic medical examination that the accused became mentally ill after the commission of the crime, and that he therefore cannot follow the proceedings, the court will interrupt the proceedings and will refer the accused to the appropriate social welfare authorities according to his place of residence. When the accused's mental health improves to such an extent that he is fit to take part in criminal proceedings, the criminal proceedings will continue. During the time when the proceedings are interrupted, during this suspended proceedings, the mentally-ill accused is provided with health care under the law under the protection of mentally ill people in the Republika Srpska or under the law of the protection mentally disturbed persons under the protection of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These laws provide for the measure of forcible detention and forcible commission to a mental health institution, and the competent entity court can issue these measures in non-trial proceedings if the person's health, life, or safety are at risk, or if the health or life or safety of others is at risk. The time during which the mentally ill person is detained cannot be longer than one year in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina or six months in the Republika Srpska. During the time when health care is being provided, the health care institution will regularly submit reports to the court and the time limit can be extended by the court in its decision pursuant to a motion by the health care institution. There is another situation. If the accused committed a crime in a state of reduced competency, the court may hand down the security measure of mandatory psychiatric treatment along with some other legal sanction. I wish to mention that at present in Bosnia and Herzegovina there are no properly equipped health institutions able to implement the measures of forcible detention and commission to a health care institution or a mental institution in cases where the person represents a serious threat to his own life, health, or safety, or the life, health, and safety of others. Efforts, however, are being made to resolve this issue. In the past year the government issued a decision to form a unit to implement a project to this effect, funds have been set aside, steps have been taken to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Ms. Popadic. So if I understand you well, finally, for purposes of trial, the jurisdiction would always be under the state court, although meanwhile an accused may be in detention somewhere else. What -- you may have noticed that the Prosecution has -- may have just -- perhaps I will just finish my question and then invite you to answer it. You may have noted that the Prosecution expressed its -- it was surprised that no facilities would be there. I would like to ask you, the situation where an accused becomes mentally ill and has to be detained because he may create a risk for himself or for others, is not unique for any ICTY case, is it. So therefore is it -- when do you think that the matter will be resolved and how are you dealing at this moment with similar cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are medical facilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to which such persons are admitted; however, those institutions are not properly equipped. And that is the reason why, in July 2006, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued a decision to form a unit which will then implement the project of renovation of the psychiatric clinic Podromanija Sokolac. We have undertaken serious steps in that regard and there are expectations that there is going to solve this issue once and for all. The issue of the persons who have to be detained pursuant to the court decision on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any expectation in terms of time as when this facility will be available?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I really couldn't give you a -- specific dead-lines here. We are aware of the gravity of the issue, and the government is currently undertaking all necessary steps in order to resolve the issue as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then, Ms. Somers, I have one, and that will be my last question. One question for you. You referred -- you expressed some concern or some big surprise that if no Tribunal would have been there that you could not accept that Bosnia and Herzegovina would not have undertaken to try genocide cases. Is that, in your view, perfectly fair to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because since there is a Tribunal and since there is a Rule 11 bis, the question is not whether Bosnia and Herzegovina would have undertaken any genocide cases if there would have been no Tribunal, but that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina will give its view on how to interpret Rule 11 bis, Rule 11 bis with -- together with the Security Council resolutions, makes a destination between cases including genocide cases, which preferably should be heard by this Tribunal or could be referred to the states of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think that Rule 11 bis or any of the resolutions underlying Rule 11 bis say that. Rule 11 bis and the resolutions that have given it power, are urging that cases and certainly there could be hundreds of persons like the accused who participate in the crimes that go into the cases that are tried here. We are trying the highest level of people here. And while we have the life in us, we will do that. But this is exactly the kind of situation that will be faced over and over again in the future, and in fact they have -- Bosnia has undermined its own position, it has undertaken the Kravica warehouse cases, where they have thousands of persons murdered. The fact that it is part of their criminal law indicates that they can. And I have not studied the history of criminal Prosecutions in Bosnia, but if it is on the books, it must have been at some point invoked and it should not be selectively rejected for inconvenience. In fact, this is a very make or break threshold issue now for the future of referrals. After all, this institution is not indicting anymore. What also strikes me, if Your Honour will allow me to piggyback on to this, is since my learned friend opposite has indicated the situation that would arise should, let's say for the sake of argument, the severance were not granted it would be putting everyone back at square zero because it would be years, if at all, and perhaps the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different issue, it's not related to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just wanted to raise the fact that you had asked me earlier about the issue of the pending motion for severance -- or self advance issue in the appeals. Because counsel has indicated a relative -- I would say statement of agreement, perhaps -- and this is of course within counsel's providence -- province, but perhaps they are considering a withdrawal of the appeal if the position is exactly what he represents the position to be, which in our view would be a wise move, it would end up effectively moving the case forward, there would be nothing gained by the appeal being heard at this point in time, I will agree assuming that the bench accepts that the gravity is well within what can be tried and what is contemplated, the level at this point, and again the balances, if Your Honours review your own excellent jurisprudence, you will see there is nothing to prevent it. You don't have to have perfect balance of both, but things are not looked at in isolation. So I'm sorry, I did piggyback on that, and I apologise, but I hope that helps a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to give an opportunity to the representative of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the parties to make final submissions each to stay within five minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, can I hear the answer raised by Ms. Somers from Mr. Piletta-Zanin because that was the very question I was about to put to you. If your position, as you submitted in your final submission, your position -- the position of yours and your client is to favour the referral as quickly as possible, then would it not be only natural for you to withdraw the appeal in relation to the severance decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for asking the question. First of all, I do not wish to answer because it's a matter of principle, because the question is put by somebody of whom I know not whether she is the author and accomplice to the denunciation concerning my client. So I would like to put the question to the Prosecution who is at the basis of the situation causing problem and threat. I want to know whom I'm talking to, and then I would gladly answer the question. What I have never ceased saying, to be brief, is that we should have staying or suspension in the first order. The first staying depends on others and that is the answer to be given as to the mental state. Why do I give you this answer? Because this is the answer that will condition the quality on the merits I will receive -- of instructions given by my client. I think you follow me. The question put to me is a treacherous one, and I cannot give you an answer, given to my obligation. I can only answer when I have a very clean answer as to the mental state. Then I can answer all the questions you may have, and I would gladly have an answer to my question: Who gave to the media the name of Mr. Trbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's the farthest we can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then for the final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the final submissions, not taking more than five minutes each, I'd like to invite Ms. Somers, you to first address the Referral Bench. If there is nothing in addition to be said, you don't have to fill the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has requested of this Bench is to refer the indictment to BH. Based on its being a jurisdiction which is able to handle the matter, and that ability has been emphasised repeatedly in other cases involving referral. And it is our sincere hope that its abilities will continue along those veins. The -- there is no issue about level, it is agreed between the parties certainly and with Bosnia that it is appropriate. Again, only should the Chamber wish to go back into its own jurisprudence and to look carefully into what is in the Security Council resolutions, the Chamber can rest comfortably knowing that Bosnia has undertaken very serious cases that even if not qualifying the crimes as genocide, is taking those facts which are also tried here and presumably will very ably handle them. There is simply no reason that it cannot do so with this accused today. The issue of fitness is at best speculative, and it is, based on what we have heard today from BH, evident that BH, if for any accused in its system should this matter arise in the -- certainly in the war crimes domain, it will have to find some resolution, even if a permanent one is not found, it will have to use its mighty powers to find some resolution in that no one can guarantee the permanent fitness of any person who is charged. There has been no evidence and certainly no indication from what has been undertaken by forensic individuals that there is an issue. Again, repeating, and not overly repeating, but today's interaction between Your Honours and the accused confirm the suggestions that were -- the conclusions that were drawn in the report. The Registry intervention we deem not founded, and should there be concerns along this line, this is part of the criminal system. That is simply the way it is. And every jurisdiction, including this one, has to find a way to deal with it. There is no suggestion that BH cannot -- in fact, it's not clear at all, I don't think it has even suggested in its responses that it cannot be dealt with. Again, for the reasons gone into private session, it is a non-issue. We are hopeful that the procedural quagmire that we find ourselves in with the delay of what may or may not be a valid appeal, and again whether or in the competency were at issue has no impact on whether an indictment should be referred. The framework, the laws, the provisions, which is the Chamber, this Bench required in Kovacevic, the provisions are in the law, it is now up to the sovereign state to find a way of implementing them and I am sure that it will do so if the need were ever to arise, but it is certainly not evident at all anything we have seen, heard or read that need arises in this case. Again, there should be no obstacle in ordering a referral of this case to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. I'd now like to give an opportunity to you, Ms. Popadic, to give any further submissions in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the link from Sarajevo at the moment. The link is back.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina has closely followed the debate today. We remain faithful to our response filed in the written form. And we also stand by everything that we have said today. I want to emphasise that the view of the government, as formulated in its written submission and today in oral submission, pertains only to this particular case. It does not in any way affect the readiness of Bosnia and Herzegovina to prosecute war crimes. However, if this bench decides to refer this case, if this Chamber decides to refer this case to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if it is established that the accused is fit to stand trial, the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina is fully equipped to provide fair and expeditious trial in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Popadic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Your time for final submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I will need less than five minutes. The Defence counsel clearly stated that within the remit of his mandate that he was to follow the instructions given by his client. Therefore, he will have to further the request for referral, unlike what the Prosecution said. The lawyer that I am cannot claim that it is possible to refer cases of genocide without further analysis. I leave that question open as a man of law. I just underline that this seemed to be a very grave claim and as a lawyer and as a Defence counsel I must state one thing, which is of interest in the observations of the Registry. If there are threats today, possibly those that I mentioned to my communications for information to my client, if the threats come -- and I might have to ask for a closed session. Or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment? Yes, private session, I think, will do. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbic, the Referral Bench would like to give you an opportunity, if there is any need to do so, to make any additional submission. Your position is perfectly clear to the Chamber, but if anything was said which causes you to make any further remarks, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I have some very brief matters to add. I don't know whether you received the summary from the last Status Conference on the 24th of November, which dealt with my health condition. I myself did not receive the minutes or the transcript from that Status Conference, but let me reiterate what I said back then. That I am fully capable, that I am completely healthy to follow any proceedings and that it is absolutely not necessary to raise this issue again. I have had five interviews so far, and as far as I'm concerned this question has been resolved. But I see that it's being raised again and again, so let me repeat that there are no grounds whatsoever to raise the issue of my ability to follow the trial. I am fully healthy and able to follow the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbic. Then I have a few final matters. First of all, the Chamber would like to hear from the parties whether there would be any objection against disclosing to Trial Chamber II the full transcript of today's hearing because there -- a few things have been said which might be relevant for a decision on competence. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We see no issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will then consider to lift the confidentiality, but only in respect of Trial Chamber II of the whole of the transcript today. Then we -- the Chamber has noticed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but this is only as to Chamber, this is not as to other counsel in the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because other accused are not involved in any way. So just for -- for the bench. Then the Chamber can imagine that there would be a need to make further submissions, although it might well be that such need does not exist. If the Registry would like to give any follow-up to further developments in relation to what has been submitted in the 30th of November submission, the Registry will have an opportunity to do so until this Friday. Because, in the 30th of November submission, some further approaches and some further processes are announced, if this results in anything the Chamber would like to receive the submissions by this Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That would not be not a -- an ex parte matter, it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it would be confidential to the parties. And of course we will -- we do not know whether there is any need to do so, but we will look at the content of it, whether there is a need to give any further opportunity to the parties to comment on that. Then as far as the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, Ms. Popadic, if you feel that you have not had sufficient time to study the submissions made by Mr. Piletta-Zanin of Friday, the 12th of January, the French ones, then if at all you want to make further submissions on that, you have an opportunity to do so until this Friday. This then concludes this -- this 11 bis hearing. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a suggestion or an idea. You suggested that the Registrar -- or the Registry might do something. Could we also ask under these circumstances, could we also ask the Registry to tell us about the situation in terms -- what happens when a detainee is set free after having spent some time in detention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by what happens then? Whether he'll -- he will be compensated, whether he'll be free to -- I mean what terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, according to the law that prevailed before in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the code of procedure at the time, a detainee would be automatically set free after a certain period of time before the judgement, so I would like to have some clarification on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider whether we will invite the Registrar to make any such submissions -- or the representatives of the -- of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if spontaneously you would like to make any further submissions on that, you are invited to do this also by this Friday. Now this concludes this 11 bis referral hearing. We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.30 p.m.
